issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma profile, 'Medical Procedures' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the report. The memory items describe classic reliving/terror reactions, and the formulation shows a strong Memory → Triggers link, implying triggers should plausibly cue the stalking memory. 'Loud noises' and possibly 'happy families' can occur idiosyncratically, but a medical examination trigger is clinically disconnected from stalking unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere. This makes the trigger set less coherent with the trauma type and formulation.

vignette:
Mai is a 38-year-old stock broker of South Eastern Asian descent who lives with her partner in a quiet suburban neighborhood. She came to therapy after a year of escalating distress, unable to explain why her life had become so small.

The stalking began two years ago, when a former client she had briefly dated started appearing outside her office, then at her gym, then at the grocery store she visited on Saturday mornings. He left notes on her car windshield, called her phone from blocked numbers, and once, when she came home late, she found him standing in the shadows of her apartment building's parking garage, reeking of alcohol. The police were involved, but he was never charged-he had plausible deniability, he was always just there, never quite threatening enough to act on. The night that broke her, he followed her car for twelve miles, and when she finally pulled into a well-lit gas station, he rolled down his window and smiled. She could smell the whiskey on his breath from ten feet away. She drove home shaking, locked every door, and did not sleep.

What stayed with Mai was not the sequence of events but the feeling that the memory itself could not be real-that it was too extreme, too cinematic to have actually happened to her. Yet when she closed her eyes, she was back in that gas station, the terror flooding her chest as if it were happening right now. The smell of alcohol, even a faint whiff from a colleague's breath after lunch, snapped her into that parking lot. She would freeze at her desk, her heart hammering, the keyboard blurring in front of her. The memory felt so vivid, so present, that it made the world around her feel thin-and then any loud noise, a car backfiring or a door slamming in the hallway, would send her spinning back into that night, the sound merging with the memory of his car engine idling behind her.

Over the months, Mai began to organize her life around avoiding these triggers. She stopped going to the gym and instead exercised at home in silence. She asked her partner to do all the grocery shopping, and she stopped meeting friends at bars or restaurants where alcohol was served. At work, she moved her desk away from the breakroom, where the coffee machine sometimes hissed and where someone might bring in wine for a celebration. She had come to believe that the world was full of things that could pull her back into that memory, and that if she was not vigilant, she would be trapped there forever. What frightened her most was that the memory might never stop feeling real-that she would always be that woman in the gas station, helpless and alone.

The loop tightened. The more she avoided, the more her brain treated every loud noise, every happy family she passed on the street (because his family had seemed so normal, so loving, and that had been part of the trap), every whiff of alcohol as a threat. Her partner grew frustrated-he wanted to go out, to see friends, to have a normal life. Mai knew she was pulling away, but she was certain that if she let her guard down, the memory would swallow her whole. She finally sought help after a colleague slammed a filing cabinet and she burst into tears at her desk, unable to explain why. What she hopes, more than anything, is that she can learn to live in the present without the past always leaking in.
